# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
This comment does valuable forensic work, and the strongest parts confirm problems I raised about the Halden pilot. The microdata show that seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the schedule started, and that managers' ratings exceeded their own records in 19 of 23 organisations. But the conclusion goes well beyond the evidence. The abstract describes corrections that the tables don't make. The novelty argument is asserted rather than tested, even though the monthly data to test it exist. And the comment cites the Varden trial selectively, so it never confronts the one randomised result that contradicts its conclusion.

## 1. Arithmetic: mostly correct, one internal inconsistency

**These check out:**
- Table 2 rows: 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9%; 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4 / 86.1 = +10.8%.
- Hours ratios: 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 (a 14.1% fall) and 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 (a 13.9% fall).
- Real revenue: 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, a fall of about 2.6%.

**The components of actual hours don't add up.** Section 3 says pilot hours rose above the 32-hour schedule through:
- 0.7 extra hours a day on four days, which is 2.8 hours, and
- 1.6 hours logged on the day off.

That gives 32 + 2.8 + 1.6 = 36.4 hours, or about 36.6 if the extra 0.7 is measured from the 8.06-hour baseline day. The reported figure is 34.6. Something else, perhaps leave or absence, would have to account for about 2 hours. If the 36.4 figure is right instead, the per-hour gain is smaller still. The authors need to reconcile this.

**Two smaller points:**
- In section 1, six withdrawals cited workload and two cited scheduling. That's eight of nine; the ninth reason is missing.
- The novelty extrapolation is slightly off. Energy fell 0.32 SD between months three and six. Continuing that line from 0.29, it reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." Either way, extrapolating from two points is arbitrary.

## 2. The abstract claims corrections the paper doesn't make

**Attrition is never corrected.** The abstract says "Correcting the first three, the gain … falls to 10.8%," and the first three problems include attrition. But Table 2 adjusts only the output measure and the hours denominator. The 10.8% is still computed on survivors, as section 6 itself acknowledges. Either correct for attrition or fix the abstract.

The microdata may make a correction possible. Seven organisations withdrew in months one and two, after monthly output reporting had begun, so partial output data may exist for them. At minimum, the authors could report bounds under plausible assumptions about the withdrawers' output.

**Revenue doesn't affect the per-hour gain.** The abstract says four problems "account for most of the reported gain." But the revenue comparison never enters the per-hour calculation. It is a separate point about how the secondary outcomes were presented.

## 3. Table 2 changes the sample and the correction at the same time

Each row uses a different subset (61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations). Moving from one row to the next changes both the correction and which organisations are included, so the differences between rows can't be attributed to the corrections.

Organisations with time-tracking software and output records are likely concentrated in particular sectors, such as professional services and software. Those are the sectors where Halden reported the largest gains. The direction of any bias is therefore unclear.

What would help:
- Run all four specifications on the same 17 organisations.
- Reweight to the full pilot's sector mix.
- State whether means are weighted by employees, as in the original, or by organisation.
- Report intervals. With 17 organisations, the 10.8% is quite uncertain.

The data note acknowledges the subset problem, but the conclusion then generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" anyway.

## 4. Some record-based measures measure input, not output

Among the record types listed is "billable hours delivered." For professional-services firms, billable hours largely track hours worked, so the measure will fall almost automatically when hours are cut, even if each hour is used better.

Some of the 3.8-point gap between managers' ratings and records may therefore reflect the measure rather than manager optimism. The authors should report Table 1 by record type, or leave hours-based records out.

The finding still holds up fairly well. Managers' ratings were higher in 19 of 23 cases, which has a sign-test p-value of about 0.003.

## 5. The novelty argument is untested even though it could be tested

The case rests on energy scores falling from month three to month six, plus the observation that staff chose and welcomed the change. But:

- **Halden collected output monthly.** If the residual gain is a novelty effect, output per hour should fall across months one to six in the microdata. The authors have the data and don't report this check.
- **Energy is not output.** A decline in self-reported energy doesn't show that productivity declined.
- **"Burden of proof" cuts both ways.** It is reasonable to say a durable effect hasn't been shown. "Entirely an artifact … of novelty" is a positive claim, and it needs its own evidence. Adding "in our assessment" doesn't change that.
- **Varden weakens the novelty story.** Its offices were randomly assigned, staff didn't choose the change, and the gain persisted at nine months.

## 6. Varden is cited selectively

**The comment relies on part of Varden and ignores the rest.** It calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." The same trial also randomised case-processing offices and reported:
- 12.5% more output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4),
- output measured from administrative records,
- actual hours taken from timesheets,
- no self-selection by offices, and nine months of follow-up.

That design rules out three of the comment's four explanations: selection, manager-reported output and scheduled hours. Only novelty remains possible. The comment doesn't mention this result. As things stand, its central claim that reduced-hours gains are "entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the study it calls most reliable.

**It also overlooks a matching finding.** In Varden's case-processing offices, output per employee was close to unchanged (−2.1%, CI −6.8 to +2.6). The comment's conclusion lists only the negative finding.

**The meetings critique misdescribes what Varden did:**

| The comment says | What Varden reported |
|---|---|
| The offices were "selected for analysis after the results were known" | The seven offices were the entire treated case-processing stratum, not a chosen subgroup |
| The analysis was fitted after the results were known | Meeting data were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results |
| It is being "cited as a mechanism" | The authors said explicitly that it cannot establish a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test |

The underlying statistical concern is fair: r = 0.71 across seven offices gives p ≈ 0.07. But the meetings explanation rests on more than that correlation:
- Varden's timesheet and calendar data imply that treated staff lost only about 5% of their non-meeting hours. On these figures, most of the per-hour gain can be accounted for without assuming novelty.
- Halden's own interviews found that 47 of 58 managers mentioned cutting meetings.

Meetings are therefore a live alternative to novelty, and the comment needs to address them rather than set them aside.

## 7. The parts that hold up well

- **Attrition (section 1).** The withdrawal timing and exit reasons contradict the working paper's account. That is an important correction and should be put to the original authors.
- **Hours (section 3).** Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%, consistent with Varden's 13–17%. This is strong evidence that scheduled hours overstate the reduction.
- **Sectoral claims (section 5).** Pointing out that any index above 80 shows up as a per-hour gain is correct. The comparison between Halden's retail results and Varden's counter stratum is suggestive rather than precise, for three reasons:
  - Only three retail organisations had records.
  - Halden has no control group.
  - Varden's −11.4% is a difference-in-differences estimate per employee, so the two figures are not like for like.
- **Revenue (section 4).** The inflation point is right. Price indices for each sector would be a better deflator than consumer prices, and revenue says little about non-profits.

## 8. A conclusion the evidence would support

> The Halden pilot's 23.4% figure is substantially overstated. In the organisations where correction is possible, record-based output and actual hours reduce the implied gain to about 11%, before any adjustment for non-random attrition, which would likely lower it further. Whether the remainder reflects novelty, process changes such as fewer meetings, or a durable effect cannot be settled with six months of uncontrolled data. Randomised evidence from Varden suggests per-hour gains of about 12% in work not tied to presence, and losses of output and service in coverage-bound work.

The recommendations in section 8 are sound: record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, longer follow-up, and analysis of all enrolled organisations.

I can draft a referee report on this comment, or a short synthesis of the three documents and what they jointly support.
